ਮੇਰਾ ਗੁਰੁ ਪਰਮੇਸਰੁ ਸੁਖਦਾਈ ॥:
Declares that the Guru is identical with the transcendent Lord, the supreme bestower of all peace and comfort. Praises the Guru not as separate teacher but as divine presence itself, source from which all happiness and inner ease flow. Affirms the oneness of Guru and God, asserting devotion to the Guru as devotion to the Supreme Being who grants peace.

Themes: Guru as divine, transcendent Lord, giver of peace, oneness of Guru and God, praise, refuge in the Guru, source of happiness, divine grace
ਤੁਮ ਦਾਤੇ ਤੁਮ ਪੁਰਖ ਬਿਧਾਤੇ ॥:
Direct address to God, praising the Divine as sole giver of all gifts and blessings, the all-pervading being present within every creature, and the architect who shapes destiny and creates all beings. A declaration of divine sovereignty over sustenance and fate—affirming that both worldly provision and the ordained course of life flow entirely from the one supreme source, present everywhere.

Themes: divine as giver, God as creator, divine providence, all-pervading presence, destiny ordained by God, praise of the Divine, sustainer of all beings
ਕਰੁਣਾ ਮੈ ਕਿਰਪਾਲ ਕ੍ਰਿਪਾ ਨਿਧਿ ਜੀਵਨ ਪਦ ਨਾਨਕ:
Addresses the Divine directly as the embodiment of compassion, mercy, and the treasure-house of kindness, pleading for the blessing of darshan (divine vision/glimpse). States that this vision itself grants the supreme state of spiritual life — liberation while living, exalted inner life attained through beholding the Divine. It is a prayerful plea combined with a declaration: seeing the Divine face is not merely comfort but the very rung of elevated spiritual existence, the goal and fulfillment of human life. Nanak names himself as the supplicant seeking this grace.

Themes: divine mercy, compassion as divine nature, darshan (vision of the Divine), plea for grace, liberation in life (jivan mukti), supplication, spiritual elevation, treasure of kindness
ਤੂੰ ਭਾਰੋ ਠਾਕੁਰੁ ਗੁਣੀ ਗਹੇਰਾ ॥੨॥:
Praises the Divine as the great Master, vast and unfathomable, an ocean deep with virtues. Declares the Lord's greatness beyond measure—full of every excellence, profound in nature, depth that cannot be plumbed. A statement of exaltation and awe, affirming divine supremacy and the boundless, treasure-like richness of qualities held within the Supreme Being.

Themes: divine greatness, God as Master (Thakur), ocean of virtues, unfathomable depth, praise and exaltation, divine excellence, awe before the Supreme
ਦੇਵਣਹਾਰੁ ਦਾਤਾਰੁ ਕਿਤੁ ਮੁਖਿ ਸਾਲਾਹੀਐ ॥:
The Divine is praised as the ultimate Giver and Provider who sustains all beings, yet the speaker confesses inadequacy: no mouth, no words are sufficient to fully praise such boundless generosity. This is an expression of humility before the Divine's greatness, acknowledging human limitation in the face of infinite grace, and implicitly a devotional yearning to praise despite this impossibility.

Themes: divine generosity, humility before God, inadequacy of praise, God as sustainer and provider, limits of human speech, devotional yearning, awe at divine grace
ਤੇਰੇ ਕਵਨ ਕਵਨ ਗੁਣ ਕਹਿ ਕਹਿ ਗਾਵਾ ਤੂ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਗ:
This line praises the Divine as infinite treasure of virtues, expressing the devotee's overwhelmed inability to enumerate them all. It is an act of awed adoration, questioning rhetorically which qualities to sing and recount because they are countless. The speaker addresses the Divine directly as Master and Lord, sustainer of all, whose excellence exceeds any single description or list, prompting continuous praise rather than complete cataloguing.

Themes: divine praise, infinite virtues, awe and wonder, Lord as treasure of qualities, rhetorical questioning, devotional surrender, inexpressibility of divine glory, sustainer of all beings
ਰੇ ਬਉਰੇ ਤੁਹਿ ਘਰੀ ਨ ਰਾਖੈ ਕੋਈ ॥:
Direct address to the deluded mind, calling it mad or foolish for its attachment to worldly life, warning that when death comes no one—no family member, no household—will let it stay even a single moment longer in the home it clings to. The tone is admonishing and cautionary, exposing the false security of household attachment and possessions, stripping away the illusion that one's dwelling or kin offer permanence. It functions as a wake-up call, urging awareness of mortality and the futility of clinging to maya (worldly attachment) and domestic ties, since the body's stay in this world and this house is fleeting and not within anyone's control to extend.

Themes: admonishing the mind, mortality, impermanence of home and household, futility of attachment, warning against delusion, maya, death's inevitability, false security
ਕਾਹੇ ਮਨ ਤੂ ਡੋਲਤਾ ਹਰਿ ਮਨਸਾ ਪੂਰਣਹਾਰੁ ॥:
Addresses one's own mind directly, questioning why it wavers, wobbles, or loses steadfastness in doubt and anxiety. Reassures that the Divine is the fulfiller of all hopes, desires, and inner longings (mansa), so there is no need for restlessness or instability. A calming admonishment urging trust and steadiness by reminding the mind that its deepest wishes are already cared for by the Lord.

Themes: instructing the mind, wavering and doubt, trust in the Divine, fulfillment of desires, inner steadiness, self-admonishment, faith over anxiety, reassurance
ਰੇ ਮਨ ਤੂ ਭੀ ਭਜੁ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ॥੨॥:
Direct address to one's own mind, urging and instructing it to remember and vibrate upon the Divine, the Lord of the universe. Follows examples of others who found liberation through such remembrance, now turned into a personal exhortation: the mind itself must take up this practice of simran (loving remembrance), not merely observe it in others. A call to inner discipline and devotion.

Themes: addressing the mind, self-exhortation, simran, remembrance of God, meditation instruction, personal spiritual duty, inner discipline
ਮਨ ਮੇਰਿਆ ਅੰਤਰਿ ਤੇਰੈ ਨਿਧਾਨੁ ਹੈ ਬਾਹਰਿ ਵਸਤੁ:
Addresses one's own mind directly, instructing it that the treasure of all happiness—the Divine—already dwells within, so there is no need to search outside, in forests or external places, for what is already present inside. A self-admonition against seeking spiritual fulfillment through external means, pilgrimage, or outer ritual, redirecting attention inward toward self-realization and the presence of the divine treasure already housed in the heart.

Themes: mind as audience, inner divine presence, treasure within, futility of external search, self-instruction, inwardness over outward ritual, self-realization, redirecting seeking
ਸੁਣਿ ਬਾਵਰੇ ਤੂ ਕਾਏ ਦੇਖਿ ਭੁਲਾਨਾ ॥:
Direct address admonishing the mind, called mad or deluded, for losing itself in the sight of worldly maya (attachment to material illusion). It commands attention—"listen"—before rebuking: gazing at transient appearances has caused the seeker to stray from the true path of life. The tone is urgent correction, warning against being fooled by outward show and worldly infatuation, calling the wandering self back to sense before it is too late.

Themes: admonishing the mind, delusion by maya, warning against distraction, straying from the path, direct address, worldly infatuation, call to awareness
ਸੁਣਿ ਬਾਵਰੇ ਥੀਉ ਰੇਣੁ ਜਿਨੀ ਪ੍ਰਭੁ ਧਿਆਇਆ ॥:
Addressing one's own mind as "madman" or foolish self, urging it to listen and heed this counsel: become the dust of the feet of those who have meditated on God (simran, loving remembrance of the Divine). This is an admonition urging radical humility and self-effacement before the devout, holding that union with God comes only through surrendering ego and seeking the lowly refuge of those who truly remember Him.

Themes: self-admonition, humility, dust of the feet, surrender to devotees, simran, seeking sangat, ego-effacement, path to union with God
ਲਖ ਖੁਸੀਆ ਪਾਤਿਸਾਹੀਆ ਜੇ ਸਤਿਗੁਰੁ ਨਦਰਿ ਕਰੇਇ:
This declares that a single glance of grace from the true Guru outweighs and equals the pleasures of hundreds of thousands of kingdoms. It exalts the Guru's grace above all worldly power, wealth, and royal enjoyment, asserting that inner spiritual favor surpasses any external attainment or sovereignty. The stance is one of devotion and gratitude, valuing divine/Guru's grace as the supreme source of true happiness, greater than any earthly dominion.

Themes: Guru's grace, glance of grace (nadar), spiritual fulfillment surpassing worldly power, true happiness through divine favor, devotion to the Guru, kingship as metaphor for inner joy, surrender to Guru's will, grace as ultimate treasure.
ਸਤਿਗੁਰੁ ਹੋਇ ਦਇਆਲੁ ਤਾ ਦੁਖੁ ਨ ਜਾਣੀਐ ॥:
Declares that when the true Guru (the divine teacher/guide) bestows grace and mercy, suffering ceases to register as suffering. The teeka clarifies: it is not that pain is absent externally, but that the graced person no longer perceives or feels adversity as painful—hardship loses its sting through divine mercy. States a resulting spiritual condition: grace transforms one's relationship to suffering itself.

Themes: Guru's grace, mercy transforming suffering, pain transcended, divine compassion, inner equanimity, result of grace, reframing hardship, spiritual protection
ਹਰਿ ਚਉਥੜੀ ਲਾਵ ਮਨਿ ਸਹਜੁ ਭਇਆ ਹਰਿ ਪਾਇਆ ਬਲਿ:
Describes the fourth and final round of the mystical marriage ceremony between the soul-bride and the Divine groom: having passed through the earlier stages, the mind now settles into sahaj, natural spiritual poise and equilibrium, and union with the Divine is achieved. The devotee declares devotion and self-offering, addressing the Beloved Lord directly ("I am sacrificed unto You"), marking this as the culmination of the soul's journey toward merger, where longing dissolves into steady inner peace and the Divine is realized within.

Themes: mystical marriage, four rounds of union, sahaj (natural equilibrium), soul-bride imagery, attainment of the Divine, self-surrender, culmination of spiritual journey, inner peace
ਸੁਖੁ ਪਾਇਆ ਸਤਿਗੁਰੂ ਮਨਾਇ ॥:
Peace and inner ease arise from pleasing and enshrining the True Guru within the heart. By winning the Guru's favor and internalizing the Guru's presence, one obtains all desired fruits and blessings. This declares the cause-and-effect result: surrender and devotion to the Guru yields spiritual contentment, fulfillment, and the attainment of one's true aims in life.

Themes: True Guru, inner peace, surrender to Guru, pleasing the Guru, fruits of devotion, heart's enshrinement, spiritual fulfillment, cause and result
ਸਤਿਗੁਰੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਸਦਾ ਸਹਾਈ ਜਿਨਿ ਦੁਖ ਕਾ ਕਾਟਿਆ:
Declares devotion and gratitude toward the true Guru (spiritual teacher/guide), affirming him as constant helper and support. States that the Guru has severed the very root/banner of suffering — the teeka clarifies this as cutting the comet/ominous star (bodi vala tara) said to bring misfortune, meaning the Guru eradicates the root cause of pain entirely for anyone who takes refuge in him. Expresses personal testimony: this Guru has become my everlasting support, removing sorrow at its source rather than merely easing symptoms. A statement of trust, refuge, and thanksgiving.

Themes: Guru as refuge, eternal support, destruction of suffering's root, surrender to the Guru, protection from misfortune, gratitude, personal testimony of grace, spiritual guide's power.
ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਮਿਲਣ ਕੀ ਇਹ ਤੇਰੀ ਬਰੀਆ ॥:
This declares human life itself as the sole, urgent opportunity to unite with Govind, the Lord of the Universe. It addresses the mind or soul directly, urging seizure of this fleeting chance now, before it passes — framing embodied existence as a precious window for divine union, not to be wasted on worldly distraction. The tone is exhortative, almost warning: this birth, this moment, is it.

Themes: urgency of human birth, opportunity for union with the Divine, exhortation to the mind, preciousness of life, spiritual awakening, self-admonition, seize the moment, meeting Govind
ਪ੍ਰਾਣੀ ਤੂੰ ਆਇਆ ਲਾਹਾ ਲੈਣਿ ॥:
Addresses the mortal being directly, declaring the purpose of human birth: this life is an opportunity to earn spiritual profit, specifically the wealth of the divine Name (naam). The tone is instructive and reminding, framing worldly existence as a business venture whose true gain lies in remembrance of God (simran) rather than material accumulation. It calls the soul to recognize why it was sent into the world at all, urging purposeful living aimed at spiritual earning before the chance is lost.

Themes: purpose of human life, naam as true profit, mortal addressed directly, spiritual earning, worldly existence as opportunity, reminder of life's goal, simran as gain, admonition to seize the chance.
ਹਰਿ ਭਗਤਿ ਦ੍ਰਿੜੁ ਮਿਲੁ ਸਾਧ ਨਾਨਕ ਤੇਰੈ ਕਾਮਿ:
Instructs and pleads: meet the saints/guru (sadh) and firmly implant devotional worship (bhagti) of the Divine within the heart. Addressed to the mind/reader directly by name, declaring that only this steadfast devotion—cultivated through holy company—will ultimately serve and benefit the soul; nothing else avails in the end.

Themes: devotion, sadh sangat, guru's company, firm resolve, naam simran, purpose of life, self-instruction, ultimate refuge
ਜੀਵਨਾ ਸਫਲ ਜੀਵਨ ਸੁਨਿ ਹਰਿ ਜਪਿ ਜਪਿ ਸਦ ਜੀਵਨਾ:
Declares that true, fruitful life belongs only to one who hears the divine Name and continually chants and meditates upon it through simran (loving remembrance) — such a person lives forever, spiritually undying. All other living is deemed hollow or wasted by contrast; this is a statement of what human life is truly for, functioning as the refrain that frames the whole composition's purpose.

Themes: naam simran, purpose of human life, fruitful versus wasted existence, hearing and chanting the Name, spiritual immortality, remembrance as true living, refrain declaring life's goal
